summary: abnt44 (Abandoned but not Forgotten) is an interactive, mobile-responsive curatorial web exhibition designed for students aged 9–15 and lifelong learners that tells the true stories of six iconic pieces of NASA hardware resting on the Moon and Mars: Surveyor 3, the Apollo 11 Lunar Module Eagle Descent Stage & Lunar Laser Ranging Retroreflector, the Spirit (MER-A) and Opportunity (MER-B) rovers, the InSight geophysical lander, and Perseverance’s discarded heat shield, backshell, and supersonic parachute. Built with 100% authentic archival photography from the official NASA Image and Video Library (images.nasa.gov) and verified NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA) telemetry, abnt44 combines an interactive Launch-vs.-Surface Mass Ledger, dual-plate NASA archival story cards, a 1967–present chronological timeline, a dual Moon and Mars cartographic atlas with a simulated 2.56-second Earth–Moon laser ranging experiment, and a 6-question field quiz to reframe silent spacecraft as enduring scientific monuments rather than forgotten debris.
details:
what Does abnt44 Do & How Does It Work?

abnt44 (Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA’s Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars) is a single-page interactive digital museum and planetary heritage exhibition designed for students aged 9–15 and lifelong learners. Rather than framing deactivated spacecraft and entry hardware as "space junk," abnt44 reframes six historic NASA machines resting on the Moon and Mars—Surveyor 3, the Apollo 11 Lunar Module Eagle Descent Stage & Laser Ranging Retroreflector, the Spirit (MER-A)and Opportunity (MER-B) rovers, the InSight Mars Lander, and Perseverance’s Discarded Heat Shield & Backshell—as silent pioneers and off-world archaeological monuments.

The application works through six integrated interactive modules:

  1. Official NASA NSSDCA Launch-vs.-Surface Mass Ledger: An interactive physics explainer showing students why the rocket equation requires spacecraft to shed launch stages, heat shields, and descent engines—and how that discarded hardware continues to serve science.
  2. Archival Story Cards & Plate Switcher: Six deep-dive exhibition cards featuring multi-plate official NASA photography (Plate A / Plate Bswitcher), landing coordinates, mission stories, scientific breakthroughs, current status, poetic reflections, and "Did You Know?" facts, paired with an interactive Official NSSDCA Dossier Modal.
  3. Chronicle Timeline & Longevity Multiplier Chart (1967–2021): A chronological scrubber and visual engineering comparison comparing each explorer's originally warranted lifespan against its actual operational endurance (such as Opportunity operating 60.8× longer than its 90-sol warranty).
  4. Interactive Moon & Mars Cartographic Atlas + Apollo 11 Laser Ranging Simulation: Dual SVG orthographic globes of the Moon and Mars with clickable landing pins, synchronized telemetry readouts, and an interactive 2.56-second Earth-to-Moon Laser Ranging Experimentsimulating how astronomers bounce laser pulses off Apollo 11's passive quartz corner-cube mirrors at Tranquility Base (0.67°N, 23.47°E).
  5. 6-Question Planetary Field Quiz: An interactive knowledge check with instant archival explanations and score tracking to reinforce classroom learning.
  6. Verified Historical NASA Records: Verbatim historical plaque inscriptions and mission transcripts from Apollo 11, Apollo 12, and NASA JPL.

What Benefits Does It Have & What Is the Intended Impact?

  • Educational Clarity & Emotional Resonance: Bridges rigorous planetary engineering (telemetry, selenographic/areographic coordinates, NSSDCA catalog IDs, and entry physics) with warm, reflective storytelling that inspires empathy and curiosity in 9–15 year-old students.
  • 100% Authentic Archival Integrity: Uses exclusively authentic, public-domain NASA photographs and verified mission specifications—eliminating synthetic or fictionalized imagery so students engage with real space history.
  • Universal Offline & Classroom Accessibility: Packaged as a lightweight, zero-dependency single-page application that runs smoothly on mobile phones, tablets, and low-bandwidth school laptops both online and offline.

Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware & Software Used

  • Languages & Core Stack: Semantic HTML5, CSS3, Tailwind CSS, and Vanilla JavaScript (ES6+) architected inside a single portable index.html file with zero heavy front-end framework dependencies.
  • Typography & Cartography: Custom interactive inline SVG planetary globes (viewBox coordinate projections for Lunar and Martian landing sites), Fraunces editorial serif display typography, Plus Jakarta Sans UI body copy, and JetBrains Mono tabular telemetry numerals.
  • Data & Archival Integration: Direct integration with the NASA Image and Video Library API (images-api.nasa.gov) and the NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA) master catalog.

How Is the Project Creative & What Factors Did Our Team Consider?

  • Museum-Grade Light Theme ("Warm Archival Alabaster"): Most space websites default to pitch-black backgrounds with neon glowing UI. We deliberately chose a warm, sunlit archival museum aesthetic (#FAF8F5 warm alabaster paper, #F2EFE9 limestone cards, lunar cobalt, and oxidized Martian ochre accents) inspired by physical natural history exhibitions and printed Apollo flight manuals.
  • Age-Appropriate Sophistication: Designing for 9–15 year-olds often risks feeling overly cartoonish. We considered reading ergonomics (60ch–70ch line widths), accessible touch targets (
     on mobile), and clear vocabulary so younger students feel respected while adults find the interface genuinely refined.
